partners.mechanism_chain: AGK (HGNC:27065) —DISRUPTS→ Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/AKT signaling (GO:0008284); Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/AKT signaling (GO:0008284) —LEADS_TO→ Cataract (HP:0000521); HRAS (HGNC:4835) —INCREASES→ Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/AKT signaling (GO:0008284); Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/AKT signaling (GO:0008284) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); LRRC56 (HGNC:33450) —DISRUPTS→ Endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi transport (GO:0006888); Endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi transport (GO:0006888) —LEADS_TO→ Global developmental delay (HP:0001263). Haploinsufficiency of AGK in Sengers syndrome disrupts the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, leading to cataracts. Gain-of-function mutations in HRAS in Costello syndrome activate the same PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, leading to intellectual disability. **Proposed mechanism:** AGK (HGNC:25803) —DISRUPTS→ Mitochondrial cardiolipin biosynthesis (GO:0006642); Mitochondrial cardiolipin biosynthesis (GO:0006642) —LEADS_TO→ Sengers syndrome (MONDO:0008922); NRAS (HGNC:7929) —INCREASES→ MAPK signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-5695100); HRAS (HGNC:4837) —INCREASES→ MAPK signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-5695100); MAPK signaling pathway (REACT:R-HSA-5695100) —LEADS_TO→ Thyroid cancer, nonmedullary, 2 (MONDO:0008566). Loss-of-function mutations in AGK disrupt mitochondrial cardiolipin biosynthesis, leading to Sengers syndrome. Gain-of-function mutations in NRAS or HRAS hyperactivate the MAPK signaling pathway, contributing to nonmedullary thyroid cancer type 2. The convergence occurs at the level of the MAPK signaling pathway, which can be aberrantly activated in various cancers, including thyroid cancer, and potentially influences cellular processes relevant to Sengers syndrome phenotypes, although indirectly.

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that mutations in AGK do not affect mitochondrial function or that NRAS/HRAS mutations do not lead to hyperactivation of the MAPK pathway in thyroid cancer cells would falsify this hypothesis. _(variant: rs123456789)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared or parallel involvement of RAS signaling and metabolic pathways could reveal novel therapeutic targets for both rare developmental disorders and common malignancies.
